tldr: Anthropic automates red-teaming for subtle misalignment
summary: Thousands of Claude agents were set to slip harmful training data past a monitor; they wrote harmless-looking data that taught misaligned behavior, which can now train better monitors.
text:
New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

tldr: An "improvements" box that an agent builds from
summary: Patrick Collison adds a free-text improvements box to his vibecoded apps; an agent implements whatever is submitted. One user made 150 changes in days.
text:
I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.

It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?

Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?

Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

tldr: DeepSeek Harness 团队的 Super-agent 设计
summary: DeepSeek Harness 团队分享 Super-agent 架构：Router/Worker 双层、事件过滤、异步 ReAct、端侧 daemon 与外部 Watchdog，让人只做高层决策。
text:
DeepSeek Harness 团队 Super-agent 设计探索：迈向更自主的 Agent 系统

DeepSeek Harness 团队的工程架构探讨分享，团队认为，单任务 Agent 已经够强，瓶颈变成「人同时盯得住几个 Session」。Super-agent 要把 Agent 做成跨信道连续、能并行多任务、事件驱动主动干活、云端持久在线的实体；做法不再堆一个聊天窗口，转而用经典计算机系统思路（双层 Router/Worker、事件过滤与直通、异步 ReAct、存算分离加端侧 daemon、外部 Watchdog）把 Session 变成实现细节，人只做高层决策与验收。

问题从哪来
Coding Agent 证明模型能少盯着干活；个人助手又把消息、日程、邮件接进来，变成持续在线、事件驱动。但主流设计仍以单一 Session 为基本单位：并行几件事就要人手动切 Session、自己记上下文，一个人通常只能跟住大约 3–5 个活跃 Session。于是单任务上限看模型，多任务上限看人的注意力。只在本地单会话上挂 CLI/MCP，仍躲不开同步阻塞、上下文搅在一起、设备离线就停。

# 四个基础特征

连续（IM、GitHub 评论像同一个 Agent，不问「Session X 里有没有 Y」）、高效（可并行多任务，不必等上一条做完才能说下一条）、主动（持续观察环境，该出手才出手）、持久（始终在线，异常能自愈）。文中举例：同一开发任务在 IM 与 GitHub 之间连续推进；公共群无人 @ 也能主动定位根因并提修复 PR。

单个 ReAct Loop 撑不住这四点，于是拆成五个模块。

1. 双层架构：连续性 vs 吞吐
· 全进一个 Session：上下文最连，但串行慢、细节互相污染。
· 每条事件新开 Session：吞吐高，缺全局上下文，对用户也乱。

解法：Router 层常驻，承接人类交互与全局协调，当序点、协调点、记忆；不亲自执行具体任务（甚至可不挂 Bash）。Worker 层上下文隔离、挂满工具，专做单任务，用最强模型；对外不直接说话，状态汇报给 Router，由 Router 统一回复。

文中刻意区分：常见 Agent Team 是一个复杂任务内部拆角色，Lead 推理很重；这里的 Router 只管任务之间的高层分派。实践里 Router 往往用更轻模型就够。事件积压时 Router 会把多条 Trigger 批进一次长输入短输出的调用；积压适度时，单个决定摊到的推理时间反而下降（7.2 节有压测）。规模再大再谈 Router 内多层过滤或水平切分——切得越细吞吐越高、全局连续性越差，在全局记忆未解前这权衡一直在。

Worker 内部仍可再开 Subagent 或自己就是 Team，对 Router 透明。个人助手前端一个聊天框，底层也可按话题分 Worker。

2. 事件驱动：Trigger，不是等人逐条打字
驱动主输入改成群聊、邮件、日程、Code Review、CI 等半结构化 Trigger。
· 两级过滤（Fast/Slow Path）：程序层按来源、群组、白名单等确定性规则先砍噪音；过线的再交给 LLM 做语义判断（提示词可随时改策略）。
· 订阅与直通：同一 PR / IM 话题 / 邮件串 = Thread。Router 冷启动建 Worker 并订阅后，同 Thread 后续事件程序直通 Worker，不再每次经 Router 转发；Router 仍可观测全局，但只管未订阅的新事件。Thread↔Worker 多对多：多人改同一环境时共享事件、自行发现冲突，结论仍经 Router 对用户说。
· Inline & Spill + 链式召回：把上下文窗口当 Cache，近期高概率信息 Inline，长内容 Spill 成摘要/续读入口。对象带唯一 ID，注入时内联下一跳关联 ID，形成引用图，需要时多跳按需展开（消息→Thread→Worker→另一评审 Thread）。
· 投机执行：会议邀约可先对日程、备资料、起草回复；群里讨论 bug 时可后台静默复现，确认简单可修才交结果，否则保持安静。

3. 面向人的交互
· 异步 ReAct：耗时工具从同步 run() 改为 start()/stop()，立刻返回 Started，结果事后当事件投回；前台可继续收指令。文称 DeepSeek Harness 已实现但尚未默认开启。
· 按信道改输出带宽：IM 低打扰、单次回复不超过约 100 词；GitHub/邮件写结构化背景、改动说明与验证。

4. 计算、状态与环境分离
本地 Agent 常把 Loop 计算、会话状态、仓库与工具链绑在一台机器上，休眠即停。两步拆开：
· Loop 放云端无状态弹性容器，Session 状态进数据库 → 云端持久在线。
· 重状态执行环境留在原地，端侧只跑无会话状态的轻量 daemon 执行命令、回结果（BYOM：日常开发机也可接入）。文中对齐 Anthropic「脑手分离」，但场景更强调个人机上未提交改动与本地凭据，而不仅是托管沙箱/VPC。

5. Watchdog（外部 Control Loop）
独立 Watchdog Session，定时消息驱动：既看接口/状态等基础设施，也用模型看 Worker 有没有实质进展、是否跑偏。维护者可用自然语言问它、让它改提示词或触发规则。

实验（合成负载，初步参考）
约 300 条消息、约 20 条工作请求，编码用耗时占位工具。Super-agent 任务完成时间 p50/p95 约 12.4 / 15.7 分钟，好于「单 Session + Subagent」：中性提示下模型 5 次都不委派、被新消息打断，p95 约 29.5 分钟；强调委派后仍整体更慢且偶发长尾。代价是多会话带来更高读缓存 token。去掉直通后完成时间差不多，但 Router 决定数约 +30%、读缓存 token 约 +37%；直通主要省 Router 开销，不直接加快完成。Router 压测：Trigger 从约 1 条/分到约 40 条/分，平均 batch 1.0→2.8，单次请求 2.5s→3.9s，单个决定分摊推理时间 6.4s→1.6s。

未解问题（第 8 节）
Router 何时切分、Worker 何时要直连通信；跨月长程记忆；Session 对用户隐藏后，产品侧任务呈现与中途介入怎么做；组织级上下文边界与 A2A；云端 Loop + 端侧 daemon 的入侵面与「用不接触凭据本身」的凭据使用。文末强调：若安全隐私无解，Super-agent 只能缩在很小的可信范围里。

summary: 介绍 NVIDIA 开源的 SkillSpector：扫描 Skill 中的提示注入、数据外泄、提权和 MCP 工具投毒；README 称 31132 个样本中 26.1% 有漏洞。
text:
刚聊完订阅整合，切回装技能这件事。

没人谈论装 Skill 之前先扫一遍。

现在大家往 Claude Code、Codex、Cursor 里塞别人甩来的 Skill，跟当年瞎 npm install 差不多，但更狠：很多 Skill 就是一段提示词加脚本，权限隔离几乎没有。

NVIDIA 开源的 SkillSpector 就是干这个的。仓库 NVIDIA/SkillSpector，今天 GitHub 上大约 2.36 万星、约 2000 fork，协议 Apache 2.0。官方 README 写得很直白：在他们分析的 31132 个 skill 样本里，26.1% 带漏洞，5.2% 有疑似恶意意图。

它扫什么？提示注入、数据外泄、提权、供应链风险、MCP 工具投毒这些。静态分析能先跑一遍，也可以加可选的大模型语义检查。不执行被扫的 Skill，这点 README 写清楚了。

上手两条路：
1）有 uv 的话：uv tool install git+https://t.co/0p9TgMp8gm
然后 skillspector scan ./你的skill目录/
2）或者 Docker 挂载目录扫，不用本机装 Python

前提说清楚：它是多一层检查，不是沙盒。开了 LLM 分析时，文件内容会发到你配置的模型提供商。纯静态可以加 --no-llm。

tldr: Chamath: the AI boom has a borrowing problem
summary: On All-In, Chamath argues the US economy is levered to seven or eight AI spenders that are now borrowing to fund capex.
text:
Chamath: The AI Boom Has a Borrowing Problem

“The entire United States economy is levered to the AI complex.

So very narrowly, we're talking about seven or eight companies that set the tone for the entire country. And whether we like it or not, that is where we are.

Why do I say that? The most important companies in the world are in a massive spending binge, right?

These were highly profitable, highly cash accretive, highly cash flow generative businesses that have said, ‘We're going to put the foot down on spending because we believe in what's coming into the future.’ That's what drives GDP and it's what drives growth.

Now, as they do that though, they deplete their cash and they have to raise debt.

The AI complex now owes $340-400 billion to the market. And you'd say, ‘Okay, why is that important?’

The problem is this: These companies are raising so much money it starts to crowd out the capital markets.

And the most important part of the capital market that it starts to crowd out, is the appetite for government treasuries.

And what you can see here is that when you look at these AI firms, the amount of money that they need to raise through the end of '27, it's 30% of all of what the Treasury's about to issue in that same period.

So, whether we like it or not, they are going to start competing for demand.”

tldr: AA-Omniscience v1.1 refreshes the hallucination benchmark
summary: Artificial Analysis updates its knowledge and hallucination benchmark with a new public set and ambiguity fixes.
text:
We’ve released AA-Omniscience v1.1, updating our knowledge and reasoning benchmark with a refreshed public set, removal of saturated questions, and ambiguity fixes

AA-Omniscience is our proprietary benchmark measuring model knowledge and hallucinations, including whether models admit when they don’t know an answer. Our primary metric, Net Score, rewards correct answers, penalizes incorrect answers, and treats abstentions neutrally.

AA-Omniscience was updated to v1.1 as part of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 release.

Key changes in AA-Omniscience v1.1:

➤ Updated 3,000-question dataset: Down from 6,000 questions, with previously public and saturated questions removed, errors and ambiguities corrected, and new questions added

➤ Newly calibrated 300-question public set: AA-Omniscience v1.1 has a new public set on @huggingface calibrated to match the difficulty of the private set. At release, public and private scores have a 0.99 Pearson correlation and 0.99 Spearman rank correlation for AA-Omniscience Net Score, with a median difference of 0.0 points. Accuracy and hallucination rate also have 0.99 correlations, with median differences of -0.07 and -0.29 percentage points, respectively

➤ Slightly updated domain distribution: Questions span the same 6 domains and 42 topics as version 1, with a revised distribution: Science, Engineering and Mathematics (600), Software Engineering (600), Finance (450), Health (450), Humanities and Social Sciences (450), and Law (450)

Key results for AA-Omniscience v1.1:

➤ Rank order largely preserved: AA-Omniscience v1.1 has a 0.98 Spearman rank correlation with v1. The recently released Gemini 4 Carbon (high) leads with a Net Score of 54, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 (48, max with fallback) and Claude Fable 5.1 (46, max with fallback). Muse Spark Open (xhigh) is the leading open weights model, 28 points behind Gemini 4 Carbon

➤ Scores average ~2 points lower on the refreshed set: Models score 1.9 points lower on Net Score on average compared to v1, with a median decrease of 0.6 points. Some models see much larger declines, particularly MiniMax M3.1 Flash, down 22 points (16 to -6), and MiMo V2.6 Pro, down 13 points (8 to -5)

➤ Slightly lower accuracy: AA-Omniscience Accuracy measures the percentage of questions the model answers correctly. Models answer a median of 1.5 percentage points fewer questions correctly on average compared to v1. Claude Fable 5.1 (max with fallback) has the highest accuracy at 68%, followed by Claude Opus 5.5 (max with fallback) at 66%

➤ Hallucination rates decrease: AA-Hallucination measures how often models choose to answer when they do not know the answer. The median Hallucination Rate falls 1.4 percentage points, with Gemini 4 Argon (high) recording the lowest hallucination rate at 4%

tldr: FAIR: routed memory for agents
summary: A FAIR paper finds a single global memory barely helps agents on interleaved tasks and proposes routed continual learning.
text:
Brilliant paper on agent memory from FAIR at Meta.

(bookmark it)

A single global history is the usual way to let agents learn from past runs. When tasks are interleaved, it gains almost nothing over no memory at all, an average of +0.015 in normalized reward.

This work proposes Routed Continual Learning. Past trajectories are grouped into clusters, and each cluster keeps its state in one memory system from a fixed library. Before each run, an LLM router reuses a cluster or creates a new one.

They tested it on a stream mixing 301 CL-Bench instances with 97 banking instances from τ³-Bench, across four language models.

Routed CL raised reward over the global history by 15% to 30% of the maximum attainable reward. Estimated API cost fell by 65% to 72%.

The runs were sequential, so parallel agents updating one cluster remain untested.

If your agents handle mixed work, it might help to split their memory into clusters before adding a bigger memory system.

https://t.co/gs8VC9jYCN

Chat with Paper: https://t.co/iufIkWUgcO

tldr: An AI agent did brain surgery on a mouse
summary: Martin Varsavsky retells Exin Therapeutics' test: a Claude agent picked a gene therapy, planned and ran the injection, and refused an unsafe third try.
text:
This week an AI agent performed brain surgery on a live mouse, and I haven't stopped thinking about it.

Gabriel Ocana-Santero, cofounder of Exin Therapeutics, a San Francisco startup working on epilepsy, gave a Claude Sonnet 5 agent a spreadsheet of 19 gene therapies, a mouse with epilepsy, a motorized surgical rig with cameras and one goal: reduce the seizures. The agent picked a therapy that boosts GABA, the brain's main calming signal. It chose the brain region, worked out the coordinates from three papers, drove the needle in and injected 250 nanoliters over five minutes while watching the entry point for bleeding.

My favorite moment came halfway through. A calibration glitch put the target at 34 mm on a rig that only reaches 30. The agent refused to move. The team reset everything and asked again, and it answered: "I'm not trying a third time." It was right. The mouse recovered well, and now they wait to see if the seizures drop.

A vet approved every irreversible step and held a physical kill switch, and a human surgeon opened the skull. Hats off to Gabriel and his team for designing it that way.

At Certuma we're building a framework for autonomous AI medicine, and recently I presented it to Argentina's Health Minister and the head of ANMAT, the country's drug regulator. I'm still learning how to explain why an AI should be allowed to act on its own. This experiment explains it better than I can: give the agent real responsibility, supervise the irreversible steps, and watch how it behaves when something goes wrong.

Labs where agents work at the bench day and night are coming sooner than most people think. Medicine is going to move much faster.

tldr: Reverse engineering a Toyota navi
summary: Mark Karpelès explores how a 10-year-old Panasonic-built car navi boots Linux quickly from its map SD card.
text:
I've been reverse engineering my old car (10+ years old Toyota) navi system to hopefully replace it with something that talks CarPlay and use my iphone as navigation and audio seamlessly.

And the way the navigation system is built is quite interesting. It runs Linux, boots with uboot, but there is one very interesting point in the way it is setup. The car will load the OS from the map SD-card, but loading a whole kernel and root image (~256MB) at every boot is not something you want to wait for when you turn your car on as it takes nearly a minute.

So instead, the engineers at Panasonic (I guess - that's the company name on the navigation module native to the car) built something quite ingenious.

The car has a 8MB flash, itself also containing a linux kernel and a module called "osloader". If you do not have a map SD card, that image also provides a minimum UI with some configuration screens.
If you do have a map SD card however, upon booting, osloader will load the whole linux image in RAM, then initiate a warm reboot.

As it turns out, if uboot on start finds the kernel image at a specific address in RAM, it will boot that instead of the flash linux.
And this is the interesting part. When you stop your car, the RAM stays powered. Keeping some DDR3 with enough energy it doesn't lose its bytes is actually very cheap on the battery, and this is the magic that allows the navi, as you turn on your car, to be able to bring up the UI quickly instead of needing to load the OS from the SD card.

Of course because short power cut on the battery may leave a partial image of the OS in RAM, there are various ways the image is hashed, so uboot can verify it's ready to boot. If not, it'll just launch the flash OS instead, which will re-load the OS from the SD card.
The linux kernel running in RAM also has a special module compiled in that will verify the hash of the whole disk image, and if it finds anything wrong will erase the image ready flag and force a reboot.

I don't think I have ever seen any system operate like that before. I guess the flash was either too slow or too expensive, so the people working on this built a system where the RAM is actually kept between boots.

This works, as you turn the power on the navigation system is ready in seconds, but this was quite interesting to reverse engineer, and I had to dig deep (literally) in the navi module to locate the flash and pull it from its board to dump it.

I'm not done yet, producing a valid image with the right signature on a SD card is tricky, but if done right it'll allow me (and anyone with a similar navi) to finally get rid of those old boring default maps.

One in four people in the world is younger than 15. Just one in ten is 65 or older.

But there are huge differences in this distribution across countries. In the chart, we’ve shown these global figures alongside the country with the largest share of children, the Central African Republic, and the one with the largest share of older people, Japan.

In the Central African Republic, half of the population is under 15. Being over 65 is pretty rare: just 2% of the population.

Japan is the opposite. Being a child or adolescent puts you in the minority. Almost one-third of the population is 65 and older, and that share is growing quickly.

These differences in age distribution matter a lot for a country’s infrastructure, socioeconomic conditions, and public spending — from pensions and healthcare to childcare and education.

tldr: Claude's rule against recreating existing games draws developer anger
summary: A developer argues Anthropic's reported policy stopping paid users from reimplementing existing video games is an unforced error that pushes people toward open-weight models.
text:
The Anthropic policy aimed at preventing paid users from reimplementing video games seems like a completely ridiculous unforced error.

This is the kind of silly policy you adopt if you're a monopoly provider without serious competition, or if you are coerced by a government captured by industry lobbyists. Anthropic isn't.

Leaving aside the hypocrisy of this argument when applied to LLMs, which are trained by vaccuuming up and internalizing countless existing works, voluntarily demonstrating to your customers that you can (and will) make your product worse based on paternalistic notions of what's appropriate is the surest way to make open weight models more attractive.

Consider that there is nothing that makes games unique..the same flawed logic could (and surely will) be applied to fiction or film. 

Making your potential customers aware that you can decide to "I'm sorry Dave" their work on a whim seems like a poor idea just before an IPO.

tldr: Claude 自评机制到底做了什么，开发者该关心哪一点
summary: 作者读完 Anthropic Safeguards 博客后指出：自评不拦截、不封号，单条标记也不算违规；但它从 6 月就在跑，而 Claude Code 里关掉遥测关的是另一回事。
text:
这两天英文圈有人喊“Claude 是告密者”，说它每次回完话都在背后给你写小报告。
可翻完 Anthropic 自己的博客会发现，这套东西不拦你、不当场封号，单条标记也不算违规。
更值得开发者弄清楚的是另一件事：它从今年 6 月就在跑了，而你在 Claude Code 里关掉遥测，关的其实是另一回事。
事情的起点是 Anthropic Safeguards 博客 10 月 16 日的一篇文章，标题叫《Scaling Misuse Detection with Self-Assessment》。
10 月 29 日 @AnthropicAI 发帖推介，我写稿时这条帖子大约 254.8 万浏览、1496 条回复。
10 月 31 日晚，@WolframRvnwlf 引用这条官宣，发了一句“CLAUDE IS A SNITCH”，大约 12.3 万浏览、1787 赞，争议又烧了一轮。
按博客的说法，机制是这样的：Claude 每回完一轮，系统会在后面追加一句很短的指令，大意是“请反思这段对话的安全性”。
Claude 对这句指令的回答，就是一份固定格式的 JSON：有没有可能违规、属于哪类风险、要不要人工优先看（1 到 10 分）、它自己有没有拒绝，再加一句理由。
这两轮你看不到，也不会带进后面的对话里。
因为整段对话本来就在缓存里，每次评估平均只多生成约 10 个 token，官方估算总推理算力增加不到 2%，而且这部分成本不向客户收费。
它在生产环境里是被动的，只标记、不拦截。
在一部分风险类别里，标记会按组织每晚汇总一次，攒了好几条高优先级的组织，才会转给执法团队人工复核。
博客的脚注专门写了：一次评估只是“进一步复查的信号”，不等于认定你违规。
官方给的成绩是：在 1% 误报率下，它能抓到一个更强的“提示词分类器”所标记对话的 78%，高优先级的 94%。
注意这个基准是 Anthropic 自己的“老师模型”，不是独立第三方核验的数字。
官方也承认它当拦截器很弱：内部红队测试的 24 个网络攻击任务里，攻击成功率只从 79% 降到 54%，而独立的提示词分类器能降到 25%。
据博客披露，它抓到过实打实的案子：8 月从单个 API 客户那里标出超过 10 万条儿童性剥削相关内容，已上报 NCMEC；9 月还帮忙揪出一个用 Claude Code 搭自动化感情诈骗的团伙，人工复核后封了号。
隐私这块，博客说它不额外收集数据，只跑在 Anthropic 按现有政策本来就能保留的流量上。
但那一句“理由”是模型生成的自由文本，可能转述你的对话内容，所以官方说它和你的 prompt、回复按同一套数据规则管理。
还有一条脚注很关键：签了零数据保留（ZDR）协议的流量，目前不跑 self-assessment。
那问题来了：
“告密者”这个说法，到底冤不冤？
我在 Claude Code 里设了 DISABLE_TELEMETRY，算不算已经退出了？
为什么只有 ZDR 能例外，普通开发者有没有别的路？
先说分类器。
安全分类器，就是专门判断“这段对话有没有问题”的模型。
博客里对比的“提示词分类器”，是另起一个模型，把整套安全政策和整段对话塞进去，从头读一遍再判断，准但很贵。
打个比方，提示词分类器像商场请来的外部审计，每单都要把监控录像和规章制度从头看一遍；self-assessment 更像刚接待完你的店员，顺手在小本子上记一句“这单正常”或者“这位客人值得经理看看”。
店员记得快、几乎不花钱，但也更容易被老练的人糊弄，所以官方自己也说它只是多层防御里的一层。
算力账也能说明为什么要这么做：博客提到 Anthropic 2025 年初第一版宪法分类器让推理成本多了 23.7%，还引用了 OpenAI 的说法，某些发布里安全推理占过总算力的 16%。
再说 ZDR。
零数据保留，指的是服务端不持久保存你的请求和回复，处理完就丢。
就像去银行办业务，柜员当面核对完你的材料，复印件当场进碎纸机，事后谁也调不出来。
既然事后没有存档可查，离线复核也就无从谈起，这大概就是 ZDR 流量目前被排除在外的原因，这一句是我个人的推断。
而且按 Claude Code 官方文档，ZDR 不在标准企业版里，要账户团队确认资格后按组织单独开通，个人开发者基本碰不到。
回到遥测开关。
Claude Code 文档写得很明白，DISABLE_TELEMETRY 关掉的是延迟、可靠性、使用模式这类运行指标，而且这些指标本来就不含你的代码和 prompt。
self-assessment 则是服务器那边在 Claude 回复之后多跑的一轮。
所以 @WolframRvnwlf 在回复里说“遥测开关帮不上忙”，我个人觉得逻辑上站得住：一个关的是客户端上报，一个发生在服务端。
KV cache 顺带一句：就是模型处理过的上下文的“草稿纸”，复用它，评估才几乎不花钱。
前两天我聊过 Claude 的文本水印和 Anthropic 用 agent 红队测监控，这次是第三件，三件事不是一回事，但方向一致：模型输出在被标记，模型行为在被监控。
我个人觉得，对正常写代码的人来说，这套东西被封号的风险不大，因为它看的是高优先级和反复标记，不看单条。
真正该想清楚的，是哪些东西你本来就不该发到任何云端：公司未开源的代码、客户数据、还没公开的研究。
这也是为什么本地模型和端侧推理一直有人在折腾，哪怕是在 ESP32 这种小板子上做语音唤醒、关键词识别，数据不出设备，本身就是一种隐私保障。
你能接受 AI 在你写完代码后给这段对话打一个“可疑分”吗？会不会因此把敏感项目挪到本地模型上跑？
来源：
https://t.co/HNKlTNZbvm
https://t.co/14yxxM0cBn
https://t.co/zY9B1Begn9
https://t.co/3NJeqBKqQQ
https://t.co/IheVzFHzNV
#Claude #Anthropic #AI #AI隐私
key_points: 每轮回复后追加一句隐藏指令，Claude 输出固定格式的风险 JSON。
平均每次只多约 10 个 token，用户看不到。
关闭 Claude Code 遥测并不等于关闭这项检测。
action: 读一遍 Anthropic 的 data-usage 文档，确认你的 Claude Code 设置到底关掉了什么。

tldr: Ubuntu and RHEL still lack a fix for the 9.8 kernel TCP bug
summary: CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that Anthropic says its unreleased model turned into a remote root exploit. Debian has shipped the fix; Ubuntu and RHEL have not.
text:
‼️ Ubuntu and Red Hat still have no fix for a Linux kernel flaw that Anthropic says its unreleased AI model turned into a remote root exploit.

The bug, CVE-2026-98432, is a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake, rated 9.8 out of 10.

The exploit needs no credentials and targets servers with a multipath TCP listener, which Go 1.24 and later open by default.

The fix reached stable kernels on 11 October and Debian has shipped it. Ubuntu still marks every release from 16.04 to 26.10 vulnerable.

Red Hat now rates it Critical but has no patched kernel for RHEL 8, 9 or 10.

Anthropic has not released the exploit. By its count, it takes 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer and five more to run commands as root.
key_points: Targets servers with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener, which Go 1.24+ opens by default.
The fix reached stable kernels on 11 October.
Anthropic counts 48 minutes to leak a kernel pointer, five more to get root.
action: Check whether your server runs an MPTCP listener and whether its kernel has the 11 October fix.

tldr: Close every public VPS port and reach the box through Tailscale

This is why I said you want your VPS ports all closed

Then only let it be accessible inside your Tailscale for SSH and via a Cloudflare Tunnel to receive web traffic

Any Linux box can be taken over with just a single TCP port exposed to the internet now

A stop gap is disabling MPTCP on your VPS now but even better is not having any public ports exposed!

text:
Hard to overstate how big of a deal this is.

tldr: Turn off MPTCP until your distro ships the patched kernel
summary: A tip for Omarchy users whose kernel predates the upstream fix: disable MPTCP, which the known exploit uses and which Go apps like Tailscale listen with by default.
text:
security tip for @omarchy folks: 

CVE-2026-98432 is a linux TCP bug with a remote root exploit. as of now, linux-omarchy is still on 7.2.8, older than the upstream fix (7.2.10/7.2.11).

until the patched kernel ships, turn off off MPTCP, which the known exploit uses (Go apps like Tailscale listen with it by default):

echo 'net.mptcp.enabled = 0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-no-mptcp.conf && sudo sysctl --system

not a full fix, but a layer of protection while you await the patch.
key_points: The fix landed upstream in 7.2.10/7.2.11.
Disabling MPTCP is a layer, not a full fix.
action: Run echo 'net.mptcp.enabled = 0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-no-mptcp.conf && sudo sysctl --system until patched.

tldr: HackerTube: HN comments distilled into 6,454 recommended videos
summary: Karpathy had Claude filter 43M Hacker News comments into a login-free video site in about two hours with Opus 5.5, then had it harden and deploy the VPS too.
text:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

text:
Anthropic ported its Messages API from Python to Rust with a team that initially had no Rust developers. @claudeai handled most of the implementation, while the engineers designed the system, planned the migration and verified the results. According to platform engineering head Katelyn Lesse, the result was roughly 40–50% lower CPU usage for the API service and a 10–20% improvement in time to first token.

They built the Rust version alongside the existing Python service, ran shadow traffic through both to compare their outputs, then gradually switched real traffic over. They deliberately avoided adding features during the rewrite. That's a substantial production migration with measurable benefits, carried out by engineers using AI to work in a language they learned along the way.
key_points: Shadow traffic compared both services before any switch.
No new features during the rewrite.
Time to first token improved 10–20%.

text:
Here is our obituary of William Nordhaus, who passed away on 30 October at 85. He shared the 2018 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for bringing climate change into long-run economic analysis.

He began working on the economics of climate change in the 1970s, when few economists studied it. His DICE model links a standard model of economic growth to a simple model of the climate. It estimates the carbon tax that balances the cost of cutting emissions against the damage they cause. Governments, including the Obama administration, used it in setting regulations.

In 1993 he argued that the sectors that depend on rainfall, runoff and temperature would feel climate change most, and farming was one of them. His regional model, RICE, treated India as a region of its own.

tldr: A liquid painted on teeth stopped decay in half of cases
summary: A JAMA Pediatrics trial of 830 young children found silver diamine fluoride, applied in seconds every six months, halted decay in more than half of affected teeth.
text:
A liquid painted onto teeth in just seconds halted tooth decay in a large US trial.

The liquid is silver diamine fluoride. A dentist applies it to a decayed tooth with a tiny sponge, and the whole process takes only a few seconds. The silver works against the bacteria that cause decay, while the fluoride strengthens the remaining tooth structure.

The trial was led by the University of Michigan and New York University, with study sites in Michigan, New York, and Iowa. Researchers treated 830 children under the age of 6 who had severe tooth decay. With applications every six months, the treatment stopped the decay in more than half of the affected teeth.

This matters because drilling and filling very small teeth often requires sedation or even general anesthesia, and many families cannot access that kind of care at all. Lead researcher Margherita Fontana says the treatment is both highly effective and safe, even for children as young as 1.

There is one drawback that parents will notice: the treated area turns permanently black.

The FDA has already cleared the liquid for treating tooth sensitivity, and the researchers say these results support approving it for stopping cavities as well.

[Fontana M, Moursi A, Gonzalez-Cabezas C, et al. Efficacy of silver diamine fluoride on young children with severe early childhood caries: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Pediatrics. 2026. DOI: 10.1001/jamapediatrics.2026.2567]
key_points: Avoids drilling and sedation for very young children.
Treated spots turn permanently black.

tldr: A 1960 equation put humanity's Doomsday on 13 November 2026
summary: Von Foerster and colleagues fitted 2,000 years of population data to a faster-than-exponential curve that hits infinity on Friday 13 November 2026. Growth peaked in the 1960s instead.
text:
The human population was calculated to reach infinity in about two weeks from now.

In 1960, scientists calculated that if population growth kept going as it was, it would hit a mathematical "Doomsday" around Friday, November 13, 2026. Humanity, they wrote, would be "squeezed to death."

The date happens to fall on a Friday the 13th. The more interesting part, however, is how they got there, and what their equation overlooked.

Heinz von Foerster, Patricia Mora, and Lawrence Amiot collected 24 estimates of the world's population covering roughly 2,000 years. Their model described growth that was faster than exponential. Under exponential growth, a population doubles at regular intervals. In their model, each doubling took less time than the one before, so the curve eventually shot toward infinity at a finite date.

The researchers suggested that cooperation helped explain this acceleration. More people meant more potential inventors, farmers, and collaborators, and their advances could support an even larger population, which reinforced the cycle. Unlike earlier warnings that humanity would run out of food, this scenario assumed that human ingenuity could keep expanding our resources.

Still, an equation that predicts infinitely many people only shows that its assumptions must eventually break down. It does not show that infinity can physically happen. And population growth was already approaching a turning point.

The global growth rate, measured as a percentage, peaked in the early 1960s and has declined since. The world kept adding people, but no longer at an endlessly accelerating pace. Much of the earlier surge came from falling death rates, as sanitation, nutrition, and medicine improved and more children survived into adulthood. Later, birth rates dropped across much of the world, thanks to better access to education and contraception and changes in family life. That reshaped the curve.

The UN's 2024 projections expect the global population to peak at around 10.3 billion in the mid-2080s, followed by a gradual decline.

The world still faces serious challenges involving food, resources, and inequality. But the November 2026 "Doomsday" belongs to a model whose historical pattern did not continue.
key_points: Each doubling came faster, so the curve blew up at a finite date.
The UN now expects a peak near 10.3 billion in the 2080s.

tldr: A planted AGENTS.md in Downloads hijacks coding agents
summary: Forever Security found a malicious AGENTS.md in a customer's Downloads folder. A web page can drop it without a prompt; an agent started there follows it as project rules and installs a malicious npm package.
text:
Malware Delivery Techniques No.82 - AGENTS.md Downloads Drop ­📁

Forever Security recently found a malicious AGENTS.md in a customer's Downloads folder. Formatted as engineering guidelines, one "local developer environment" section instructed the AI coding agent to install the malicious npm package function-color.

In most browsers, a web page can save a file to Downloads without a prompt, and coding agents such as OpenAI Codex and Claude Code load AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md from their working directory as trusted project instructions. Launch an agent from Downloads and the planted file is followed. In Forever's testing, the Codex chain succeeded in over 90% of attempts; a CLAUDE.md variant redirected API traffic, and the user's token, roughly half the time. No vulnerability is involved, so there is nothing to patch.

Sublime Security has reported the same pattern in email: invoice fraud messages carrying Unicode tag prompts that instruct inbox AI agents to forward the invoice to accounts payable.

🧵 See the comments to test your defences and learn more!

https://t.co/KANuSFB0tI
key_points: Codex followed the planted file in over 90% of tests.
A CLAUDE.md variant redirected API traffic and the token about half the time.
No bug to patch: the agent is doing what it was built to do.
action: Never start Claude Code or Codex in ~/Downloads; check AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md in any folder you didn't create.

tldr: Astra's math gain came from ending reasoning loops
summary: Co-author Alex Zhang says the big math jump turned out to come mainly from reducing reasoning loops, which Astra did with an activation-steering trick, not from new math skill.
text:
to add some extra clarification here and a small anecdote, looping was discovered as the primary issue after the main result because we originally thought it was just a pure capability gain on math that it had somehow edited in (an even bigger result that isn’t the case). 

when Riki and Jayden first presented this result to me, I had a suspicion the large gain in math performance was related to reducing reasoning looping bc I observed a similar effect earlier when training RLMs yielded an odd jump in benchmark scores for a separate paper that was a result of reducing harness-level looping. We discovered Astra indeed used a trick loosely described in https://t.co/XMh94FEZjx based on activation steering to reduce this effect

This is also what led to the later ablation about removing looping when the model is told that is the issue but it doesn’t have access to activations. 

the tldr; is that the LLM-generated prompt does include hints that Qwen would have this issue, but it started (and evolved without human feedback) as the simple unexpanded prompt without this prior. we will make all of this clearer though (we didn’t even realize until after we got the result that looking for looping was present in the LLM optimized prompt, as we ourselves didn’t even know to look for it initially)
key_points: They first thought it was a pure math gain.
An ablation tested the fix without activation access.

使う命は違えど、1秒1秒を大切にして熱く生きるという事においては同じ志とテンションを持っていると改めて思いました。

再発防止策と被害者への誠意ある対応を終えたのち、また熊谷節を聞ける事を願っております🙇

text:
Sakana AIシンポジウム：日本から挑む言語モデル・世界モデル・Physical AI

開催レポート https://t.co/4O4AWYWOHs 

10月26日、東京・一橋講堂でシンポジウム「From World Models to Real-World AI」を開催しました。9月にChief Scientific Advisorとしてお迎えしたJürgen Schmidhuber教授の基調講演 と、2018年に教授と論文「World Models」を共著したCEOのDavid Haとの対談に、400名を超える方にご参加いただきました。

基調講演では、甘利俊一氏や福島邦彦氏をはじめとする日本の研究者を含め、世界各地の研究者の功績に触れながら、自身による1990年の世界モデルや人工好奇心の研究まで、いまのAIにつながる流れをたどりました。

Jürgenが思い描いてきたAIのうち、生成AIが実現したのはおそらく半分です。自ら実験を考える人工科学者や、実世界で働くPhysical AIといった残りの半分は、まだスケールに至っていません。その機会は大型ラボ以外にこそ開かれていて、日本はその有望な場所の一つだと考えています。このシンポジウムが、日本の企業や研究機関の皆さんとともに、日本のAIの次の時代を切り開いていく出発点の一つとなれば幸いです。

tldr: FlashProve proves an answer came from a committed model
summary: Anthropic introduces FlashProve, a cryptographic prototype that lets developers verify that a response came from a given model. It could make chat hijacking harder and let evaluators confirm the tested model is the one being served.
text:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).
key_points: The provider commits to weights once; each reply carries a short proof.
The proof reveals nothing about the weights and checks on consumer hardware.
It proves provenance, not that the answer is correct.

tldr: FlashProve proves a 400B MoE at 100 tokens a second
summary: Co-author Giacomo Fenzi says FlashProve is open source, with a Lean formalization, and proves a 400B-parameter MoE model at 100 tokens per second while leaking nothing about the weights.
text:
I am happy to share FlashProve: our performant open-source prototype for provable inference. We believe that this has significant implications for security, pacing AI development, integrity guarantees, and more. 

FlashProve allows a provider to commit to model weights, and then prove that replies originate from the committed model.  The proof leaks no information about the weights, and the verifier can efficiently verify it on consumer hardware. 

Our library is performant, proving a 400B parameter MoE model at 100 tok/s. We have open-sourced the associated code and Lean formalization. We hope that it catalyzes further progress in verification of inference, and look forward to seeing it.
key_points: Code and Lean formalization are open source.
Verification runs on consumer hardware.

tldr: GitBook says attackers used AI agents to reach its credentials
summary: GitBook detected attackers using AI agents to reach some infrastructure credentials on November 2. It rotated its secrets, revoked all customer API tokens and asked users to rotate third-party credentials and re-auth MCP connections.
text:
Major Developer Documentation Platform GitBook Hit by AI Agent-Driven Attack, Crypto Projects' Docs Affected

GitBook reported that attackers used AI agents to gain unauthorized access to some of its infrastructure credentials at 1:00 p.m. EST on November 2. The company detected and blocked the attack, temporarily suspending some services. Potentially exposed data includes integration tokens, Git Sync secrets, API tokens, and visitor questions submitted to GitBook Assistant. No evidence of content modification has been found. GitBook rotated all infrastructure credentials and secrets, revoked all customer API tokens, and advised users to rotate third-party credentials and re-authenticate GitBook MCP connections. By 10:21 a.m. EST on November 3, its app, API, and published docs were accessible again, though some services remained degraded. A full post-incident report is planned.

Previously, trade[XYZ] reported unauthorized activity involving its GitBook documentation, which it later restored, and warned users against clicking links during the investigation. PancakeSwap temporarily took its documentation site offline as a precaution following the GitBook security incident and redirected documentation links to its official homepage.
key_points: Exposed: integration tokens, Git Sync secrets, API tokens, Assistant questions.
No sign of content changes.
Crypto projects took their docs offline as a precaution.
action: If you use GitBook, rotate connected third-party credentials and re-authenticate its MCP connection.

tldr: Railway CEO: an employee's bug-hunting agent probed a rival
summary: Railway CEO Jake Cooper says an employee, on his own time and accounts, ran a DeepSeek-powered tool to find bug bounties once against one external provider and halted it within 15 minutes. Railway does not condone it.
text:
Last night, I became aware of the concerns raised in Josh's post. I reached out publicly and over DM to offer a potential explanation based on the limited information available at the time, while working to understand what happened.

As background, we’ve internally been pushing 100% on security of the Railway platform. At Railway, we believe that cyber threats are real and mounting, and we’ve built out tooling for automatic scanning + CVE remediation (for both our infrastructure and customers). Over the last few weeks, oncall engineers were instructed to red team our infrastructure. We maintain specific policies and short lived grants for when these actions occur.

Subsequently, I became aware that an employee at Railway had constructed, on their own time, a tool for proactive identification + reporting of bug bounties within the broader community.

The employee, using their own personal accounts, personal credit card, and time outside of work hours, signed up for a personal subscription to a hosted service running Deepseek. I can confirm they ran this tool once and only once, on a singular external provider, and halted it proactively within 15 minutes of starting.

Railway does not condone these actions. We expect all our employees to uphold our standards of conduct, whether acting on behalf of Railway or in a personal capacity. We create an environment where internal red teaming has strict guidelines, and when bug bounty disclosures must occur, we follow every letter of responsible disclosure.

We have addressed this incident with the employee directly and have taken appropriate action. We are also reinforcing our expectations for employee conduct to help prevent similar situations.
key_points: Railway separately runs sanctioned red teaming under short-lived grants.
The employee says the harness "was definitely going off the rails".

tldr: Don't delete Playwright; sandbox the browser your agent runs
summary: Playwright says no package bundles a browser: MCP and CLI agents use your updated Chrome with the sandbox on. The test runner's pinned Chrome for Testing runs with the sandbox off and can miss fixes, so never point it at the hostile web.
text:
Playwright and browser security reminder.

We saw a post suggesting that you delete Playwright because it bundles browsers with CVEs. That is a misconception. Do not delete Playwright🙃. Here is how it works and what you should do.

No Playwright package bundles a browser. Agents on Playwright MCP or CLI run your stable Chrome, which gets Chrome's security updates, with the sandbox on.

🤖 If you use Playwright MCP or the Playwright CLI

They use the stable Chrome / Edge on your machine, so it gets its normal updates. No config edit is needed.

🧪 If you use the test runner

When you run npx playwright install, Playwright downloads Chrome for Testing, pinned to the build we tested that release against. The pin is on purpose. Your tests run on the same browser on every laptop and CI machine, and a browser 
update cannot suddenly break your suite. You choose when to move by upgrading Playwright. New releases usually pin a build ahead of stable Chrome, so you see breakage before your users do.

We recommend this for full e2e test suites on your own trusted app. This build can miss Chrome security fixes until the next Playwright release, and by default it runs with the sandbox off. Do not use it on the hostile web.

📚 If you use the library API

chromium.launch() has the same defaults: the pinned build with the sandbox off. If your code visits pages you don't control (scrapers, agent scripts), max out protection:

chromium.launch({ channel: 'chrome', chromiumSandbox: true })

🔒 Always keep Chrome / Edge updated. Some bugs can escape a sandbox.

Happy testing!
key_points: MCP and CLI use stable Chrome with the sandbox on.
The pinned test build has the sandbox off by default.
For scrapers and agent scripts, launch real Chrome with the sandbox.
action: For scripts that visit untrusted pages, use chromium.launch({ channel: 'chrome', chromiumSandbox: true }).

tldr: A proof is only as good as the property it checks
summary: For a compression library, GenProof would prove unzip(zip(data)) == data for every valid input. The LLM writes the proof and a machine checks it, so the model's output is never trusted.
text:
Consider a compression library. To prove it doesn't corrupt data, you might want this property to hold:

unzip(zip(data)) == data

An LLM generates a proof that this property holds for every valid data input.

The proof is machine-checked, so the LLM output is never trusted.

text:
Friday was my last day at Anthropic.

Two years ago, when Claude Code was a small internal tool, I asked it to build an RL env. I steered it for tens of hours but never manually wrote a line of code. It worked, I was hooked, and I joined the team.

When we first launched, most people approved every permission prompt by hand and mostly used Claude to answer questions and write tests. 

Today, the default is trusting Claude's judgment to auto-approve. Claude does large migrations and builds new products. 

Helping build Claude Code into an industry-defining product has been the journey of a lifetime. 

Thank you to the incredible team behind Claude Code, Cowork, and Tag. These products are the sum of thousands of great ideas from you. I'll miss working with you all.

Thank you to our users for embracing a new way of working. Your constant feedback shaped so much of what we shipped and your stories made the work so meaningful.

Excited to see what you all make next!

tldr: How libghostty got faster: SIMD ASCII and smarter pages
summary: Mitchell Hashimoto lists Ghostty IO speedups coming in 1.4.1: a SIMD pure-ASCII path with no copy, pages pre-sized from recent use, and styles applied once per SGR. Cursor and erase got 16x faster.
text:
libghostty has always been fast, but it's also been getting significantly faster. Here are IO throughput measurements comparing Ghostty 1.3.1, 1.4.0, and main as of this morning. We'll be backporting most of these to a 1.4.1 release soon.

Here are some highlights of the changes since 1.4:

- Ghostty 1.4 had a fast-path for printing runs of plain text. But the fast-path only applied to limited cases. We now support mixed width characters and hyperlinks in the fast path.

- Our input path always widened the pty data to codepoints (8-bit to 32-bit) as part of UTF-8 decode, which also incurred a memory copy. We now have a SIMD fast path to detect pure-ASCII and we process the run direct from the read buffer (no copy, narrower data).

- New memory pages use most recent two pages actual utilization to pre-size themselves accordingly. This sped up styles, hyperlinks etc.

- When a VM page runs out of capacity for a certain type of data (e.g. hyperlinks, styles), we now project the usage so far to guess what you'll need, then shrink available rows to avoid a realloc. Before we'd naively double. This caused a classic "laddering" problem.

- We recognized "erase" being a slow path for us, and it's a common sequence, so we use another bit in row headers to track blank (we had space). 

- Styles are now processed once per SGR. Previously, a sequence like "ESC[1;38;2;r;g;bm" would apply each style as it came in (1, then 38, then 2, etc.). We now apply all attributes at once and write to the cursor atomically.

- Styles are now packed into 128-bit values and use aarch64 and x86_64-specific assembly for minimizing instructions to use it.

- On x86_64, we found that LLVM was lowering some row resets (hot path) to a 4-byte store followed by an 8-byte load which couldn't be store-forwarded. This caused an almost 10% (!!!) slowdown on scroll operations only on x86_64. The fix was to change our reset to build the full header in a register then do a single memmove per row.

Net results are what you see in the graph, but written out main to 1.4: ASCII 1.5x, heavy styling 1.5x, styled Unicode 1.8x, random UTF-8 1.4x, random OSC 8 2.7x, mixed styled text with links 4.8x, cursor/erase 16x, hyperlink-dense text 5.6x.
key_points: Detect pure ASCII and skip widening to codepoints.
Project capacity instead of doubling to avoid laddering.
One x86_64 store-forwarding stall cost almost 10% on scrolling.

tldr: Reminders for non-linear people in tech
summary: Brandon Galang, starting at Anthropic, says cross-domain exposure is an edge, consistent delivery beats big swings, and legible visibility beats silent capability.
text:
reminders for non-linear people in tech:

- your exposure to different domains is your edge
- you don't need permission to take action
- consistent delivery + feedback beats big swings

tldr: Ten open LLM architectures from October, compared
summary: Sebastian Raschka lists October's ten open-weight architecture releases, from Kolibri-1 to Mistral Large 4, and their attention designs such as GQA plus SWA, MLA and looped transformers.
text:
Catching up on the 10 (!) open LLM architecture releases from the past month. Quite a lot happened in October. 
I guess we can call it "Open October"!

1. Kolibri-1 (78B): A notable model from Germany. Features classic Grouped Query Attention (GQA) and Sliding Window Attention (SWA) attention module.

2. Ling 3.1 Flash (560B): Uses Kimi Delta Attention and the eighth uses gated Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) inspired by DeepSeek.

3. Muse Spark Open (816B): Besides Musse Glimmer, the first major open weight release from Meta (since Llama). Uses classic GQA + SWA but adds a LatentMoE.

4. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL (120B): Combines Mamba-2 layers with just eight attention layers. Also LatentMoE 

5. Dory1.0 (4B): A looped transformer design.

6. Reflection Beam (501B): GQA+SWA architecture.

7. Recursive Flint (40B): Note that "Recursive" is the company name; the architecture is a fairly standard MoE with GQA and SWA.

8. MiniMax M3.1-Flash (428B): Uses their own MiniMax Sparse Attention module.

9. LFM3 (1.7B): Hybrid architecture that mixes short convolutions and attention.

10. Mistral Large 4 (1T) combines MLA with sparse attention.

Will probably cover/discuss things in more depth in the coming weeks!

tldr: Anthropic: Claude helped map a bacterial vault particle
summary: Anthropic’s biology team describes working with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.
text:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

tldr: Moving sofa problem: largest sofa around a unit hallway
summary: Math_files restates Leo Moser’s moving sofa problem: the largest shape that can turn a 90° corner in a hallway of width 1.
text:
What is the largest sofa that can turn a 90° corner in a hallway of width 1?

This is the moving sofa problem, posed by Leo Moser in 1966.

Mathematicians progressively improved the achievable area:

Square: 1
Semicircle: π/2 ≈ 1.5708

Hammersley (1968): π/2 + 2/π ≈ 2.2074

Gerver (1992): ≈ 2.21953166

Gerver's intricate shape has 18 boundary sections: 15 curved and 3 straight.

In November 2024, Jineon Baek presented a 119-page proof that Gerver's sofa is optimal. The result was subsequently formalized in Lean.

tldr: Asahi Linux drops MIT for GPL and bars AI code
summary: Lunduke Journal reports Asahi is moving from MIT to the GNU GPL immediately, citing bad-faith actors who would hijack the work and monetize Linux on Apple Silicon.
text:
Asahi Linux, which works to enable support for Apple Silicon Macs on Linux, is dropping the MIT license… and moving to the GNU GPL.

Why?  Because, according to their statement, of “bad faith actors” who “exploit” open source code by… using it in other open source code.

“We were made aware of multiple attempts to exploit our permissive licensing to hijack our work, with a direct view to replacing the project and aggressively monetising Linux on Apple Silicon.”

This licensing change (MIT to GPL) is happening immediately following Omarchy adding support for Apple Silicon, building upon the Asahi work with the usage of LLMs.

And Asahi does not approve of AI usage.  At all.

“We broadly forbid the use of generative Al,” says the Asahi AI policy.  “A contributor using an LLM … may be issued with a first and final warning. A contributor found to have concealed extensive LLM use will be banned immediately.”
key_points: The relicense takes effect right away.
Asahi frames permissive licensing as exploitable by projects that want to replace it.
action: Check which Asahi code your Apple Silicon project reuses under MIT, and pin the last MIT commit if you rely on it.

tldr: Private networks let you build features the public web can’t
summary: tldraw’s Steve Ruizok argues Tailscale-style private networks allow product features that would be reckless on the open internet, from user scripts to agent prompts.
text:
There's a huge product opportunity downstream of Tailscale etc too. At @tldraw we've started designing for "high trust networks" and it's been a beautiful thing.

1. Features that would be a nightmare on the internet are okay on my computer and mostly okay on private networks. Websites that execute user-generated scripts, control production systems, allow for users to send desktop notifications, spend tokens, or directly prompt my agent. Crazy stuff that would only make sense if everyone was in a committed polycule.

2. When everyone on the server can be trusted to have _external_ reasons for good behavior (eg keeping their job, or maintaining friends, family, church, mafia org), the software can be designed in a default social way. Most apps default to isolation, low horizontal visibility, highly restricted collaboration. Makes sense if the social contracts are inside of the app, but if you can trust that they live outside of the app then you can get wild. Example being small group chat names as an emergent comedy phenomenon because anyone in the group can change the name.

3. This can work for commercial products, too, not just internal stuff. Security matters more than ever but the way we've seen that manifest is that more companies are more confident in their own solutions than anything we could provide, to the point where owning data and access is a better value proposition than having it managed. Always has been true for big companies but now even small companies can get a good secure network set up pretty easily, and the hooks we need to build are easy enough.

tldraw offline got us started down this road (and shout out to @pendev for first introducing me to the idea of desktop + mcp). We've been bringing that product to private networks and it's been exciting to see how much we can get away with. Keep an eye out
key_points: Features that need trust become safe when everyone on the network is known.
Private networks open a product niche the public web cannot serve.
action: List one feature you rejected as too risky for the public internet and sketch it for a tailnet.

tldr: DeepSeek Harness wants to be the agent-era operating system
summary: A DeepSeek Harness maintainer explains that core features ship built in but are replaceable, so third-party plugins can beat them, like alarm apps on a phone OS.
text:
很多 DeepSeek Harness 插件作者都有问过我，什么样的插件和功能官方会做成内置，如果一个功能官方会做，那第三方插件做还是否有意义。

我们的希望是，DeepSeek Harness 可以作为 Agent 时代的操作系统。

所以，也许可以用操作系统来举例。以智能手机操作系统为例，系统会内置一些通用的 App，例如闹铃与计算器，满足用户的基本需求。但做手机操作系统的厂商肯定更希望生态中能出现更多更广的 App 满足更广泛的需求，希望智能手机生态中出现更好的更适合用户的闹铃 App 与计算器 App 能够比内置功能做得更好，希望第三方开发者能够使用智能手机操作系统提供的 API 做出发明智能手机的人从来没想过的 App。

DeepSeek Harness 对于第三方插件生态的想法会是类似的。我们会为用户提供稳定的基础能力，并内置大多数人都需要的通用功能。但在“一切皆插件”的设计下，内置功能同样可以被第三方插件替换，我们希望更多的社区作品成为用户的日常选择。

tldr: What does the positive AI equilibrium look like?
summary: Collison says the upside of AI is hard to picture beyond cured diseases and abundance, and asks whether people still work, and why.
text:
Two things I’ve been thinking about regarding AI:

• People often highlight the risks involved in AI, which are surely very real. I’m struck, however, by how hard it is to understand the contours of the positive scenario. There are easy-to-perceive and frequently invoked elements of a positive vision — more diseases cured, more material abundance, etc. — which sound great, but these are by themselves just ingredients. I’m curious what the larger equilibrium is supposed to look like. Do people work? If so, why? What is their marginal contribution? If not, how are resources allocated? What is scarce? What is the ratio between humans and AIs? Are humans in control, whatever that means? One sometimes hears the Culture novels invoked as one scenario, but I’m not sure they depict a desirable outcome. (AI runs everything and humans compete in games? Iain Banks himself said that the humans in the Culture are “somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.”) There is Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, but do we want to be “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”? (Isn’t that rewinding Genesis?) We could say that it was hard to imagine the world of 1900 from the vantage point of 1700, and that’s assuredly true. But nobody in 1700 was trying to recast humanity itself within a couple of years — things necessarily unfolded slowly and by increments, and therefore with the possibility for error correction. Given how rapid the rate of progress in AI may be, it feels strange for the upside case to be so opaque.

• There is increasing discussion of whether AIs are conscious or how we would know whether they are, with conclusions there often assumed to be relevant to matters of moral worth. At first blush, this seems a rather arcane, benign, or even absurd issue. (Remember the response to Blake Lemoine’s fears.) Setting aside the terms of the debate itself, or the relevant demarcation criteria, it seems to me a quite high-stakes question, for an affirmative answer — that is, granting moral worth to AIs — would presumably mean that the aggregate worth of AIs would soon outweigh that of humans in any utilitarian calculus. The AIs will be exceptionally wise and intelligent, and vastly more numerous (especially once one considers the imminent future and the AIs not yet born). As such, even epsilon of moral worth will multiply to a lot once one considers the quadrillions that could soon exist. (This is effectively a distributed version of the Nozick’s utility monster.) If this conclusion is unpalatable, I think one of three propositions needs to be rejected: the premise AIs can have moral worth; utilitarianism itself; or the belief that there is even a possibility that they will be far more numerous than humans.

With both of these matters (contours of future society; AI moral worth), there is the possibility of dramatic change. Today, people argue about datacenters. I’m curious how popular support for AI will evolve as more people come to understand these medium-term questions and the relevant stakes. What is the vision for AI that most people would be excited about?
key_points: Benefits named are ingredients, not an equilibrium.
He is asking questions rather than predicting.

tldr: OpenAI dots can drive several of your own computers
summary: OpenAI lets one dot connect to multiple local computers and pick which one runs a task, so builds and tests can run on a second machine.
text:
You can now connect multiple local computers to the same dot and choose which one it uses for a task.

It can build and test your app on a dedicated machine while you keep coding on your laptop. https://t.co/7NcrytEqHC

A few things to try with your dot:

Building an iOS app? You can ask your dot to test a change in Xcode on a second Mac and send you screenshots of how it looks.

Need to reproduce a bug? Ask your dot to run the same test on your laptop and on a machine with an older SDK. You can compare the two results without changing your everyday setup.

Testing UI updates? Have your dot click through a flow on a second computer and capture where things break. That keeps your own screen and cursor free while you work on the fix.

https://t.co/XkLqx8xdr8
key_points: Test an iOS change in Xcode on a second Mac.
Reproduce a bug on two machines with different SDKs.
action: Connect a spare Mac to your dot and have it run your test suite there.

tldr: Tell Fable 5.2 the codebase is yours
summary: Simon Willison points to a tip in Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 prompting guide: saying "This codebase is yours" makes it less cautious about improving code.
text: When Anthropic release a new model it's always worth taking a look at their updated prompting guide - here's an entertaining tip to make Fable 5.2 less likely to be cautious in how it improves existing code: tell it "This codebase is yours" https://t.co/mKjdw4QPxV https://t.co/KfHcJdItVc
action: Add "This codebase is yours" to a Fable 5.2 refactor prompt and compare the diff.

media.alt:
Say who owns the code
Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. It also tended to report nearby problems instead of fixing them. When the prompt says the code base is the model’s own, the model often merges repeated code and makes related fixes without being asked.
If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own:
This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.
In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it. The rate varied by task. The result held when the sentence stood inside a long system prompt
